title: Stop saying "fail": use words that describe what's happening and what to do next
summary: Jason Cohen argues "fail" is almost always the wrong word for setbacks because it is final and suggests no next step. He maps different situations (experiments, innovation, learning, optimizing, problem-solving, major errors) to more precise vocabulary that points toward action, reserving "failed" for true shutdowns.

principles.text: Words should explain what's going on and suggest the next step; "fail" does neither.
principles.quote: Words have meaning. They can explain what's really going on, and suggest what should be done next. The word "fail" accomplishes neither.

principles.text: Treat unsuccessful paths in building a business as backtracking in a maze, not failure.
principles.quote: If you're solving a maze, and a path doesn't work out, you haven't "failed," you've only backtracked.

principles.text: Frame attempts as experiments: either result is evidence, so neither is a failure, even when most A/B tests find no win.
principles.quote: The result of an experiment is evidence supporting or rejecting the hypothesis. Neither result is a "failure." A/B testing is a good practice, even though most of the time you will not have stumbled upon an improvement.

principles.text: Innovation requires many trials; an attempt that doesn't revolutionize things yet just hasn't found the breakthrough.
principles.quote: Often innovations require many trials before the right solution is uncovered. If the right answer were obvious, it wouldn't be an innovation.

principles.text: Fast-moving problem-solving in complex organizations inevitably includes setbacks; adapt rather than label them failure.
principles.quote: Problem-solving in a complex space--whether a one-person startup or a thousand-person organization--cannot possibly proceed with innovation and speed and yet also no setbacks, no complications, no false-starts.

principles.text: Even for a major misjudgment, name its nature (pivot, overhaul, redesign) so the label points to the fix; reserve "we failed" for real shutdowns.
principles.quote: Still, that doesn't explain its nature, and doesn't point towards a solution, which would be the constructive thing to do.
